lines.text: An ant with two rules builds a highway, and nobody can prove why.
This is an ant. It can't see, it can't think, it doesn't remember anything. It only knows how to do two things, and with that, it's going to build a highway.
A board of squares, and every square is a bit: on, or off.
If the ant steps on a square that's off, it switches it on and turns right.
If it steps on one that's on, it switches it off and turns left.
Then it moves forward. That's all it knows how to do.
Watch it slowly. On, turn, step. Off, turn, step.
The first few hundred steps make small, tidy shapes. Almost pretty.
And then it breaks. A thousand steps. Five thousand. A messy blob that grows with no shape, never repeating, going nowhere.
If you had to bet right now, you'd say this ends in nothing.
Step nine thousand, nine hundred seventy-seven.
Look. The ant shoots off diagonally, and starts building a highway.
A hundred and four steps that repeat. And again. And again. It never comes back. It'll keep going like this forever.
This is called Langton's ant. Chris Langton came up with it in 1986, looking for the simplest rule that could behave like something alive.
And here's the uncomfortable part. Nobody knows why.
Switch on any squares you like before it starts, wherever you want, and it happens again.
It might take longer, or less, but it ends up building the same highway. Every time. And it's never been proven.
And there's more. Set up the starting squares just right, and this ant can build any logic circuit.
A whole computer, made from a bug that only knows how to turn. Two rules. One bit. And forty years without a proof.
What do you think? Coincidence, or is there something hidden in there we still can't see? Tell me in the comments.
